title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
hookLine: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
last: BHAKTI WALKS OUT OF THE FIRE.

cards: A hunter goes into the forest and finds nothing, all day. Night falls, and he's too far from home and too stubborn to go back empty-handed. So he climbs a tree beside a pool, where animals will come to drink, and waits.
He hasn't eaten. He can't let himself sleep, or he'll fall. To keep busy, he plucks leaves off the branch, one by one, and drops them without looking where they land.
This is one of the stories told on Maha Shivaratri: a man who keeps the festival perfectly without knowing it exists.

teach.b: Shiva-ratri: the night of Shiva, the fourteenth night of the waning moon in late winter. The hunter's tree was a bilva, whose three-part leaves are sacred to Shiva.

And under it, hidden in the dark, was a lingam, the simple rounded stone that stands for Shiva in temples and shrines. All night his dropped leaves fell on it, and drops from his water pot spilled on it.
He fasted, because he had no food. He stayed awake, because he had to.

teach.h: BILVA LEAVES FALL ON A HIDDEN LINGAM.
teach.b: Without meaning to, he had done what Shivaratri asks: fast, keep vigil, offer water and bilva leaves to the lingam.
In the Shiva Purana's telling, deer come to the pool through the night, and each one asks to be spared long enough to go home first, and the hunter, softening, lets them go.

By dawn, the story says, his heart is changed, and Shiva's grace reaches him. And here's the teaching devotees love in it. Shiva is called Bholenath, the innocent lord, and Ashutosh, the one quickly pleased.

teach.h: A FAST AND A VIGIL, BY ACCIDENT.
teach.b: A few leaves, a little water, a night without sleep, given even by accident, reached him.
You don't need to be learned to begin; you need to show up. That's why temples stay open until morning, full of people who may know only five syllables.
Devotees pour water, milk and honey over the lingam, a rite called abhisheka, and repeat na-mah shi-va-ya, Om Namah Shivaya, bowing to Shiva, until the sky gets light.

how: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, visit Shiva temples, pour water or milk over the lingam with bilva leaves, and keep vigil through the night repeating Om Namah Shivaya; many temples stay open until dawn.

s: the hunter keeps the festival without knowing it
he fasts, stays awake and drops bilva leaves and water on a hidden lingam.
Maha Shivaratri falls on a full-moon night
it falls on the fourteenth night of the waning moon, the last dark before the new moon.

a few leaves and a little water, offered even by accident, reached him.

games.q: you're the hunter, hungry after a day with nothing. a deer comes to the pool and asks to go home first, promising to return. what do you do?
o: climb down and chase her off.
games.why: in the Shiva Purana's telling he lets the deer go, softening through the night, and by dawn Shiva's grace reaches him.

practice: Sit upright, the way the hunter had to on his branch. On each slow breath out, say the five syllables, Om Namah Shivaya, or if you don't pray, simply count the breath.

When the first urge comes to stop, to check your phone, to be done, stay for three more breaths. If there's a little water nearby, end the way the hunter did without knowing: pour a few drops onto a plant, as a small offering.

wordCard.voice: Shivaratri. The night of Shiva, kept with fasting, water and bilva leaves on the lingam, and Om Namah Shivaya until dawn, for the lord who is quickly pleased.

orig.note: Sanskrit: om, namaḥ (bowing to), śivāya (to Shiva). na-maḥ-śi-vā-ya is the five-syllable mantra.

carryVoice: Your line: Ashutosh, Shiva is quickly pleased. The hunter found it by accident. Good night, for now.
